title: Proofreading & Fidelity Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll watch DNA polymerase proofread its own work — and meet the mismatch-repair team.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology DNA Replication — proofreading via 3' to 5' exonuclease, mismatch repair, mutations and replication fidelity.
final_note: You learned that DNA polymerase has a 3' to 5' exonuclease that proofreads, mismatch repair fixes remaining errors, and rare mistakes become permanent mutations.

walkthroughs.body_html:
DNA polymerase III selects bases by complementarity — but it sometimes pairs the wrong one (about 1 in 10⁵).

That's not good enough. After proofreading + mismatch repair, the error rate is ~1 in 10⁹.

For a human genome of 3 × 10⁹ bases, that's only ~3 errors per cell division. Impressive.

DNA polymerase has a second activity: a 3' to 5' exonuclease.

When the polymerase senses a mispaired nucleotide just added (poor base-pair geometry), it:
1. Stalls
2. Reverses direction
3. Snips off the wrong base with the exonuclease
4. Tries again with the correct nucleotide

It catches ~99% of its own mistakes.

After replication, mismatch repair proteins scan for missed errors. They can tell new from old strand (old strand is methylated). The new wrong base is excised and re-synthesised.

What polymerase can't fix is the end of a linear chromosome — RNA primer can't be replaced. So each round, the chromosome shortens.

Telomeres are repetitive (TTAGGG) caps that buffer this loss. Telomerase can extend them — active in germ cells and most cancers.

When telomeres run out → cell senescence or apoptosis. A natural counter on cell divisions.

options: The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.
